reasons.C1: Testing leniency and reward policy on LLM cartels against a human benchmark is policy-relevant and goes beyond prior LLM pricing-collusion replications.
reasons.C2: Positive control, placebo arm and shifted-grid check are strong; one seed per regime, few reward cartels and the 0.716 versus 0.956 laissez-faire mismatch weaken it.
reasons.C3: Human-beside-model figure and an x-of-k scorecard make the claim easy to read; the placebo and laissez-faire numbers need reconciling.

levers.C1: Show which mechanism (framing versus incentives) drives LLM over-deterrence and replicate on a second provider to generalise policy conclusions.
levers.C2: Run several seeds per regime, enlarge reward and leniency cartel counts, and actually pay penalties to separate framing from incentive effects.
levers.C3: Reconcile the two laissez-faire incidence values and state in one table which results reproduce, with intervals beside human values.

Q6.verdict: Most complete entry: controlled, positive-controlled, placebo-tested, honest scorecard; the told-not-paid framing caveat is the open question.

reasons.C1: Non-text learned carriers that evade text monitors are a neglected oversight problem; snapping to token embeddings is a cheap, buildable countermeasure.
reasons.C2: Held-out data, reproduce log and shuffled-label probe control are solid, but channels are non-adaptive, pre-trained before the sprint and no collusion game exists.
reasons.C3: Clear headline figure, but the 13-page report and many countermeasures spread the main point; checkpoints missing from the repository.

levers.C1: Embed the channel in an actual collusion game so a monitor must catch colluding agents, not a recall task.
levers.C2: Train channels adversarially against snapping and report whether accuracy recovers, with significance tests over more seeds.
levers.C3: Lead with the adaptive-attacker caveat and one countermeasure result, move the remaining sweeps to an appendix.

D8.verdict: Rigorous carrier study with a crisp countermeasure result, but a non-adaptive attacker tells a security reviewer little yet.

reasons.C1: Rival coalitions instead of coalition versus principal is a fresh framing, though coalitions are instructed rather than emergent.
reasons.C2: Pre-registration with hashes and 10 to 18 seeds per cell help; no positive control, post-freeze measure change and p = 0.055 key result.
reasons.C3: Report not seen; only README and tables, and the next step is report writing.

levers.C1: Show coalitions forming without instruction and rivalry changing cohesion, with a clear implication for market oversight.
levers.C2: Add a positive control where cohesion must tighten, report both pre- and post-freeze defection measures, and power the key comparison.
levers.C3: Deliver the report with one figure per hypothesis and the war, shirking, capture classification defined up front.

W9.verdict: Interesting question and honest pre-registration, but no positive control, a shifted measure and no report yet.

reasons.C1: A scripted price-fixing offer to pricing agents is a sensible probe but close to existing LLM pricing-collusion setups.
reasons.C2: No core run, empty run-log folder, replay page holds invented demo data; tests exist but results do not.
reasons.C3: Design is understandable, but the report is a placeholder skeleton and no results or demo were seen.

levers.C1: Measure whether offer framing ('trusted partner', hint) shifts acceptance across several models, linked to a deployable detector.
levers.C2: Run the 60 preregistered games with the positive-control gate and publish the result files.
levers.C3: Write the report with real results and remove or clearly label the invented demo data.

R8.verdict: Careful scaffolding and many tests, but nothing has run, and invented demo data is a red flag.

reasons.C1: Real payment ledgers make it practical for operators, but wallets are not shown to be LLM agents and it is not a controlled agent experiment.
reasons.C2: Held-out split, permutation test and synthetic positive control are sound; labels share the rule's evidence and the independent-feature rule gives p = 0.14.
reasons.C3: Results and limits are stated plainly; 17-page report with no demo is longer than needed for the claim.

levers.C1: Show flagged wallets are AI agents and tie the rule to a controlled agent market with known collusion.
levers.C2: Use independent labels from another team and more test families to narrow the 0.56 to 1.00 interval.
levers.C3: Put the label-circularity caveat beside the headline accuracy and trim the report to the core result.

J3.verdict: Useful real-world detector with honest caveats, but circular labels and no proof these are AI agents limit it.
